| Dataset | Campaign | Period | Location | Range | N records |

| Grenfell & Light (2007) | SHEBA 1998 | Apr 8 – Sep 3, 1998 | ~76°N Arctic Ocean | 400–1000 nm | 56 |
| Smith et al. (2021) | MOSAiC Leg 4 | Jun 13 – Sep 19, 2020 | ~82°N Arctic Ocean | 350–2500 nm | 44 |

Both datasets acquired via portable ASD-type spectrometers on sea ice.

## Interpretation

### Snow performance

Both datasets pass the build-spec criteria (|BBA Δ| ≤ 0.05, RMSE ≤ 0.10). Grenfell spring snow (Apr–May 1998) shows a consistent positive visible bias of +0.031 — the model is slightly too bright, consistent with the snow grain radius (200 µm) being slightly too small for old metamorphosed Arctic snow. Smith MOSAiC snow (June 2020) shows a visible bias of +0.257 and NIR bias of +0.301 across 400–1000 nm. June snow at 82°N is warmer and more metamorphosed than April SHEBA snow, consistent with the larger grain sizes implied by lower visible albedo.

### SWIR window (Smith data, 1000–2400 nm)

The Smith dataset extends to 2400 nm, covering the strong water/ice absorption bands at 1.5 µm and 2.0 µm. Mean SWIR RMSE (1000–2400 nm) = 0.193. The model tends to overestimate in the 1000–1300 nm window (shallow NIR absorption shoulder) and underestimate in the 1300–1500 nm transition. Performance in the 1500–1800 nm window is better because absorption dominates and the spectral contrast between configurations is lower.

### Dataset comparison

Despite being collected 22 years apart, at different latitudes (76°N vs 82°N), and in different seasons (Apr–May vs Jun), the two datasets show broadly consistent model performance. Smith 2020 snow is darker (lower VIS) than Grenfell 1998 spring snow, consistent with warmer/more melted conditions in June. The model's FYI_WINTER_SNOW preset sits between the two, which is physically reasonable: it is calibrated for winter/early-spring but not specifically for either dataset's exact conditions.
